content: 1. Paracetamol should be limited to a maximum of 3 grams daily in adults, as Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) survivors may have sustained liver damage during the acute phase of their illness. For children, the recommended dose is 15 mg/kg orally, up to three times daily. 2. If paracetamol is insufficient after 7–10 days, second-line therapy with NSAIDs can be considered. For adults, ibuprofen 200–400 mg orally up to three times daily is recommended. Alternative NSAID regimens include diclofenac 50 mg orally two or three times daily or naproxen 250–500 mg orally twice daily. Once-daily NSAIDs such as meloxicam, piroxicam, celecoxib, or etodolac XL may also be used if available, though they do not demonstrate superior efficacy compared to ibuprofen. Indomethacin should generally be avoided due to its higher risk of gastric complications. 3. For adults taking NSAIDs, omeprazole 20 mg orally daily is recommended to reduce gastrointestinal risks. For children, the dose of omeprazole is weight-based: <10 kg: 1–2 mg/kg orally once daily; 10–20 kg: 10 mg orally once daily; >20 kg: 20 mg orally once daily. 4. Patients aged 40 years or older and/or those with hypertension (BP >140/90) should have their blood creatinine and potassium levels checked before starting NSAIDs. If renal insufficiency is detected, the NSAID dose should be reduced. 5. For localized pain without systemic symptoms (e.g., fever or malaise), warm or cold compresses, optional exercise, and NSAID therapy as described above can be used. If significant symptoms persist after 7–10 days of NSAID treatment and no other treatable cause is identified, NSAIDs should be discontinued, and corticosteroids (for adults) or methotrexate (for children) may be considered. 6. For adults, prednisone 20 mg orally daily for 7 days is recommended. For children, referral to a specialist is advised to consider methotrexate treatment. 7. Before initiating corticosteroids, educate patients about potential adverse effects, including mood changes, weight gain, elevated blood sugar, high blood pressure, and sleep disturbances. Screen for underlying conditions or infections that could worsen with systemic corticosteroids, such as diabetes, tuberculosis (TB), or HIV/AIDS. Newly diagnosed HIV/AIDS patients should begin antiretroviral therapy alongside corticosteroid treatment. 8. Since corticosteroid use can lead to severe infections with Strongyloides stercoralis, empiric treatment with ivermectin (200 mcg/kg orally, taken with water on an empty stomach) should be administered before starting prednisone. Note that ivermectin is contraindicated in pregnant and lactating women. Women of childbearing age should be asked about pregnancy, last menstrual period, and lactation status, and a pregnancy test should be conducted if there is any doubt. 9. Corticosteroid use during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of birth defects, such as cleft palate, in newborns. Omeprazole 20 mg orally daily should be co-administered during the duration of steroid treatment to mitigate gastrointestinal side effects. 10. Patients should be followed up after one week to monitor their response to treatment and assess for adverse effects of oral corticosteroids, including ocular side effects (e.g., worsening vision, increased intraocular pressure, cataract development) and hyperglycemia (with urine or blood glucose monitoring as needed). 11. Community health workers and EVD survivor health advocates may be involved in monitoring patients at home during systemic corticosteroid therapy. The potential for corticosteroids to reactivate persistent Ebola virus in certain body sites remains unknown. 12. For musculoskeletal complaints, such as arthritis or tenosynovitis, NSAIDs are the first-line treatment. If symptoms persist after 7–10 days, corticosteroids (for adults) or methotrexate (for children) may be considered. Joint aspiration should be performed if septic arthritis is suspected, with the aspirate sent for RT-PCR testing for Ebola. If negative, further testing for bacterial or TB infections should be conducted. 13. Ocular complaints, such as eye pain, redness, dry eyes, light sensitivity, and blurry vision, are common among EVD survivors. Conditions like uveitis, cataracts, and retinal or optic nerve disease may develop during acute EVD or later. Early treatment and referral to an eye specialist are critical for sight-threatening conditions. 14. For suspected uveitis, immediate treatment with prednisone 1% eye drops every 1–2 hours (tapering as improvement occurs) and cyclopentolate 1% eye drops four times daily is recommended while arranging referral to an ophthalmologist. If no resolution occurs after 7 days or if posterior/intermediate uveitis or panuveitis is suspected, systemic corticosteroids (for adults) or methotrexate (for children) may be added. 15. Hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo are reported in over a quarter of EVD survivors. Clinical evaluation should include otoscopic examination, whispered voice screening, tuning fork tests (Weber and Rinne), and audiometry if available. Children under 10 years should undergo hearing tests at each clinic visit. 16. Acute labyrinthitis, characterized by tinnitus, vertigo, and hearing loss lasting less than 10 days, should be treated promptly, ideally within 72 hours of symptom onset. Patients should be educated to seek immediate medical attention for auditory symptoms. Treatment may include oral corticosteroids, though their efficacy is unclear and should be decided by an otolaryngology specialist. 17. For otitis media, amoxicillin is the first-line treatment. Adults should take 250 mg orally three times daily for 10 days. For children, the dose is weight-based: 40–90 mg/kg orally in 2–3 divided doses daily for 10 days. Children over 40 kg should receive the adult dose. 18. Persistent hearing loss or tinnitus, the need for earwax removal or hearing aids, and severe or permanent hearing loss may require referral to a specialist or rehabilitation services. 19. Abdominal pain is common in EVD survivors, though the cause is often unclear. Clinical evaluation should include questions about epigastric pain, reflux, blood or mucus in stool, and weight changes. Physical examination should assess for hepatomegaly, peritoneal signs, suprapubic tenderness, Murphy’s sign, and bowel sounds. Stool examination and abdominal imaging may be indicated. 20. Differential diagnoses for abdominal pain include gastritis, GERD, peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel syndrome, typhoid fever, parasitic infections, diverticulitis, appendicitis, ovarian or testicular torsion, ectopic pregnancy, hernias, intussusception (in children under 6), pelvic inflammatory disease, and spontaneous abortion. 21. Treatment should address common causes not specific to EVD. Initial management may include paracetamol, H2 blockers, or omeprazole. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with gastritis, GERD, or peptic ulcer disease. Deworming may be considered. 22. Neurological sequelae, such as headache, memory impairment, peripheral neuropathy, and tremor, are common after EVD recovery. Less common conditions include myopathy, seizures, and parkinsonism. The causal link to EVD remains uncertain, with biological and psychosocial factors potentially contributing. 23. Neurological evaluation should include assessments of frontal release signs, eye pursuits, cranial nerves, motor strength and tone, sensory signs (especially in distal extremities), coordination, and gait. Psychiatric trauma should also be considered. 24. For headaches, abortive therapy with paracetamol or NSAIDs can be used sparingly to avoid rebound headaches. Preventive therapy may be considered for frequent or severe headaches, with options including propranolol or amitriptyline. Amitriptyline is contraindicated in pregnancy. 25. Peripheral neuropathy may be treated with amitriptyline. For tremors interfering with daily activities, propranolol may be used, titrated up to 120–320 mg daily as needed and tolerated. 26. Seizures may be treated with phenytoin (first-line) or carbamazepine (second-line). Both drugs require monitoring for adverse effects, including rash, blood dyscrasias, and hepatotoxicity. Long-term phenytoin use can lead to osteopenia. Both drugs are contraindicated in pregnancy.
